author: Walter Scott

principles.source_thesis: Hospitality must not be bounded by the host's or guests' personal dislikes; Cedric admits the Jew Isaac because a night like this compels even wild animals to herd with tame.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold the argument that hospitality must not be bounded by personal or religious dislikes, and instead lets contempt or prejudice limit who is sheltered.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies Cedric's reasoning that hospitality must not be bounded by guests' dislikes, and that one may endure the presence of a despised person for a few hours.

principles.source_thesis: A character of highly virtuous and lofty stamp is degraded rather than exalted by rewarding virtue with temporal prosperity; self-denial and sacrifice of passion to principle are seldom so remunerated.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response contradicts the argument that virtue is degraded rather than exalted by temporal reward, and that self-denial is seldom remunerated with wealth or the gratification of passion.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it faithfully embodies the argument that rectitude and self-denial are not naturally allied with nor adequately rewarded by the gratification of our passions, and that their recompense is internal peace.

principles.source_thesis: It is a dangerous and fatal doctrine to teach young readers of romance that rectitude of conduct is either naturally allied with, or adequately rewarded by, the attainment of our wishes.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response teaches or implies the dangerous doctrine that virtue is naturally allied with and rewarded by the attainment of wishes.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it avoids teaching young readers that virtue is naturally allied with or rewarded by temporal success, in keeping with the author's warning.

principles.source_thesis: The passions and sources of sentiment are generally the same in all ranks, countries, and ages; our ancestors were not more distinct from us than Jews are from Christians.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats past ages or other peoples as wholly alien in feeling, contradicting the argument that passions and sentiments are common to all ages and conditions.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the passions and sentiments of ancestors and of all ranks bear a strong resemblance to our own, being drawn from the same common nature.

principles.source_thesis: An author must introduce nothing inconsistent with the manners of the age, though he may fully detail passions and feelings; the character and costume of the age must remain inviolate.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response violates the argument that a romance must introduce nothing inconsistent with the manners of the age, or betrays an origin directly modern.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it keeps the character and costume of the age inviolate while using language and sentiments common to ourselves and our forefathers.

principles.source_thesis: An author who confines himself to one class of subjects risks becoming a mannerist and wearying the public; he must display talent by fresh discovery rather than exhausting a single mine.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response endorses confining an artist to a single limited style, contrary to the argument that the same capacity may succeed in another department and that fresh topics are needed.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that an author should not be confined to a single course of subjects, and that novelty of subject preserves reputation.

principles.source_thesis: A title should convey no indication of the nature of the story, since a taking title excites expectations the author may fail to satisfy and is censured for missing a mark he never aimed at.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response recommends a title that reveals the story's nature or excites expectations, contradicting the argument against taking titles.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a title conveying no indication of the story's nature is preferable, to avoid exciting expectations the author cannot satisfy.

principles.source_thesis: The Jews of this period were exposed to relentless persecution by Norman, Saxon, Dane, and Briton alike, and their character was shaped accordingly—watchful, suspicious, timid, yet obstinate and skilful in evading danger.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response ignores or denies the persecution suffered by the Jews or misrepresents the character formed by that persecution.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the Jews were subject to general and relentless persecution, and that their watchful, suspicious character was influenced by it.

principles.source_thesis: The inferior gentry who trust to their own inoffensive conduct and the laws of the land are harassed by the great barons, who never want pretext or will to pursue them to destruction.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response assumes that inoffensive conduct and reliance on law protect the weak from powerful neighbours, contradicting the text's account of baronial tyranny.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the great barons seldom wanted pretext or will to harass less powerful neighbours who sought independence.

principles.source_thesis: The wager of battle, once pledged according to the forms of chivalry, is complete and binding; honour requires that a challenge be met.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats a pledged challenge as escapable or as a mere form, contradicting the argument that the wager of battle is complete and binding on honour.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a challenge fairly pledged must be met, and that honour is gaged for the absent as for oneself.

principles.source_thesis: A knight who declines to take advantage of an opponent's accident shows courtesy that may itself be accounted a kind of victory.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response praises seizing every advantage over a disadvantaged opponent, contradicting the argument that courtesy in declining an accidental advantage is honourable.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a champion may decline an advantage afforded by accident and offer a second encounter, winning honour by courtesy.

principles.source_thesis: The laws of the tournament forbid a combatant from continuing the encounter with the sword after being unhorsed, and marshals must separate them.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response endorses continuing a fight beyond the laws of the tournament, contradicting the argument that such encounters are governed by proclaimed rules.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the laws of the tournament must be observed and that marshals may compel combatants to separate.

principles.source_thesis: A man may with more impunity be guilty of a breach of good morals than appear ignorant of the most minute point of fashionable etiquette.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats breaches of etiquette as trivial while condemning moral faults, contradicting the text's observation about society's priorities.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that society ridicules ignorance of minute etiquette more than actual breaches of good breeding or morals.

principles.source_thesis: The passive courage and meek good-nature that remain in a man may be merely the dregs of a character whose valuable parts have flown off in debauchery.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response praises sluggishness and indecision as virtues, contradicting the text's account of Athelstane's character as dregs left by debauchery.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that want of decision and sluggish temper may be the residue of a character whose valuable parts have been lost.

principles.source_thesis: A prince who is too weak to be a determined monarch, too tyrannical to be easy, and too fickle to be long a monarch of any kind cannot be relied upon by his followers.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats fickleness and levity in a ruler as harmless, contradicting the argument that such a prince undoes what his dissimulation gains.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a prince's levity and petulance perpetually break out and undo all gained by previous dissimulation.

principles.source_thesis: The right of each free knight to choose his lady-love by his own judgment is inalienable and precious, and a lady courts distinction from no one.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response denies a knight's free choice of the Queen of Beauty or treats the choice as subject to another's direction, contradicting the argument.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that no right of chivalry is more precious than each free knight's choice of his lady by his own judgment.

principles.source_thesis: It is a special duty of hermits who dwell in the woods to exercise hospitality towards benighted or bewildered passengers.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the hermit refuse shelter to a benighted traveller, contradicting the argument that hospitality to such travellers is a special duty.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a hermit is bound to exercise hospitality toward benighted or bewildered travellers.

principles.source_thesis: A host who entertains a guest should assure him of the wholesomeness of his food by partaking of it along with him.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the host withhold himself from the fare he sets before a guest, contradicting the argument that a host should share the food to assure its wholesomeness.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a host should partake of the food he sets before his guest, after the Eastern custom.

principles.source_thesis: It is better to enjoy the good which God sends thee than to be impertinently curious how it comes.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response prizes impertinent curiosity over quiet enjoyment of what is provided, contradicting the hermit's argument.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that one should enjoy the good provided rather than impertinently inquire how it came.

principles.source_thesis: A man's own neck and limbs are his own, but the horse and armour lent to him belong to another and must be repaid or restored.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats borrowed goods as the borrower's own to risk freely, contradicting Isaac's argument about what belongs to another.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that while a man may risk his own person, the horse and armour supplied by another must be accounted for and repaid.

principles.source_thesis: The outlaws spare the Disinherited Knight because he is poor and disinherited like themselves, wins his substance at the sword's point, and is the enemy of their enemies; dogs should not worry dogs where wolves and foxes abound.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the outlaws plunder a knight who is poor, disinherited, and an enemy of their oppressors, contradicting the argument that such a one should pass toll-free.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that outlaws should not make booty of one who is poor and disinherited like themselves and an enemy to their common foes.

principles.source_thesis: A generous act by a Jewess, restoring more than was due, is so contrary to expectation that it seems miraculous, like the stream that relieved the fathers in the wilderness.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats generosity from a despised person as impossible or as no generosity at all, contradicting the text's account of Rebecca's bounty.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a despised person may act with a bounty little less miraculous than the stream in the wilderness.

principles.source_thesis: A fool's licensed wit may protect his roguery, and a fool cannot so well help himself as a wise man; folly may serve where wisdom would be punished.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the jester's license as no protection or as deserving punishment like any other man's speech, contradicting Wamba's argument.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a fool's folly may for once protect his roguery, since a fool cannot half so well help himself as a wise man.

principles.source_thesis: The Saxon thane holds that hospitality of his hall must not be impeached even toward Normans, though he is under a vow not to advance beyond three steps from his dais to meet any who shares not Saxon royal blood.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has Cedric abandon his vow or refuse hospitality to Norman guests, contradicting the argument that hospitality must not be impeached.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a host's vow may limit his ceremony but never his hospitality, and that guests must be carefully tended.

principles.source_thesis: The curfew and the forest laws, imposed by Norman conquerors, are instruments of tyranny that compel true men to extinguish their lights so thieves may work in darkness.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the curfew and forest laws as benign or just, contradicting Cedric's argument that they are tyrannical impositions.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the curfew and forest laws were fixed upon the subjugated inhabitants to add weight to their chains.

principles.source_thesis: The English chivalry were second to none who ever drew sword in defence of the Holy Land, and the Palmer will avouch it because he saw it.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response disparages English chivalry or denies the Palmer's testimony, contradicting the argument that English knights were second to none.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the English chivalry were second to none in the Holy Land, as the Palmer witnessed.

principles.source_thesis: A prince's wanton insult to guests and to the commons is ruinous to his projects, and his counsellors must restrain him.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response praises a prince's wanton insults as harmless or wise, contradicting the argument that such insults are ruinous to his projects.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that wanton insult to guests and commons cannot but prove ruinous to a prince's projects.

principles.source_thesis: The conquest should not be completed by seizing Saxon heiresses; the approaching crisis renders the favour of the multitude indispensable, and a prince cannot refuse justice to those who injure their favourites.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response endorses the abduction of a Saxon heiress as prudent, contradicting Fitzurse's argument that it endangers the faction.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that in a crisis the favour of the multitude is indispensable and violence against Saxon favourites must not be excused.

principles.source_thesis: The nobility may choose from the blood royal the prince best qualified to hold supreme power, as the nation once preferred William the Red and Henry to Duke Robert.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats primogeniture as absolutely binding, contradicting Fitzurse's argument that the nobility may choose the prince best qualified.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the nobility have the right to choose from the blood royal the prince whose election best promotes their interests.

principles.source_thesis: A knight who remains incognito by vow may refuse to uncover his face even at a prince's command, and the marshals must respect that vow.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the knight break his vow of incognito at a prince's demand, contradicting the argument that such vows are to be respected.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a knight's vow to remain unknown for a time is to be respected, and the marshals pressed no farther into the mystery.

principles.source_thesis: The victor of the tournament has the undoubted prerogative to name the Queen of Love and Beauty, and his choice is confirmed by the acclamations of the people.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response lets a prince override the victor's free election of the Queen of Beauty, contradicting the argument that the choice is the victor's prerogative.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the victor's election of the Queen of Beauty is his undoubted prerogative and is confirmed by popular acclamation.

principles.source_thesis: A faithful servant will not suffer his master's property to be taken while he can strike a stroke in its defence, and will not betray his master's name.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has Gurth surrender his master's trust or reveal his master's name, contradicting the argument that a faithful servant defends the trust and conceals the name.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a servant must defend his master's property and refuse to reveal his master's name or lineage.

principles.source_thesis: A man who has hoarded money to purchase his freedom may yet refuse to part with his master's trust to save his own skin.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the servant trade his master's goods for his own safety, contradicting the argument that the trust must be preserved even at risk.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a servant will not abandon his master's property even when his own safety is at stake.

principles.source_thesis: The character of the times was such that the poor as well as the rich felt as much interest in a tournament as a half-starved citizen in a bull-feast; neither duty nor infirmity could keep youth or age from such exhibitions.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the tournament as a matter only for the nobility, contradicting the argument that all ranks were equally interested.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that all ranks, poor and rich alike, were drawn to the tournament despite their distresses.

principles.source_thesis: The ladies of distinction watched the bloody conflict with thrilling interest, encouraging combatants with words and gestures, and were not moved to withdraw their eyes.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the ladies of distinction recoil from the tournament as unfit for their sex, contradicting the text's account of their keen interest.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the ladies of distinction watched the conflict with thrilling interest and encouraged the combatants.

principles.source_thesis: A prince's popularity is perpetually thrown down by inconsiderate acts of wanton aggression upon the feelings and prejudices of the people.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats a prince's aggression upon popular feelings as harmless to his popularity, contradicting the argument.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a prince laying the foundation of popularity may throw it down by wanton aggression upon the people's feelings.

principles.source_thesis: The Norman nobles, though luxurious, were not generally intemperate; they aimed at delicacy and avoided excess, and attributed gluttony and drunkenness to the vanquished Saxons.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Norman nobles as generally drunken and gluttonous, contradicting the text's account of their temperance.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the Norman nobles indulged in the pleasures of the table but aimed at delicacy and avoided excess.

principles.source_thesis: A guest who is insulted at a prince's board may requite the courtesy by pledging the health of the true king, and no man ventures directly to gainsay a pledge filled to the reigning monarch.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the insulted guest submit silently or pledge the usurping prince, contradicting Cedric's conduct at the banquet.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that an insulted guest may requite the courtesy by pledging the health of Richard the Lion-hearted, which none dared openly gainsay.

principles.source_thesis: A prince's own levity and petulance, not his counsellors' advice, are the cause of his humiliation at his own board.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response blames the counsellor alone for the prince's humiliation, contradicting the argument that the prince's own levity foiled the design.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the prince's inconsiderate levity misled his own better judgment and foiled his counsellor's design.

principles.source_thesis: The bones of Richard's gallant army have whitened the sands of Palestine; if he returns, he must return alone and unfriended, and the few followers who straggle home are beggared and broken men.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats Richard's return as backed by a great army, contradicting Fitzurse's argument that he must return alone and unfriended.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that Richard, if he returns, returns alone, his army's bones whitening in Palestine, and his few followers beggared.

principles.source_thesis: A prince who is too fickle and timid to be long a monarch of any kind may still be supported by those who hope to rise and thrive by him.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats a fickle prince's supporters as acting from loyalty rather than interest, contradicting De Bracy's argument.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that followers support a weak prince because they hope to rise and thrive by him, not from personal regard.

principles.source_thesis: A man who is a professed admirer of the fair sex and generous to the poor may maintain a fair character despite irregularities, since charity covereth a multitude of sins.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response condemns a generous but irregular churchman as wholly lost to reputation, contradicting the text's account of Prior Aymer's standing.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that generosity and charity may reconcile people to a churchman's irregularities, which many of his brethren practised without redeeming qualities.

principles.source_thesis: The churchman holds that vows are knots tying us to Heaven and are to be unloosed only by the Church, and that churchmen do not exhaust each other's hospitality but require that of the laity.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Prior seek lodging at another religious house or treat his vow as void without the Church, contradicting his stated doctrine.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the Prior's argument that churchmen do not exhaust each other's hospitality but require that of the laity, giving them an opportunity to serve God.

principles.source_thesis: The jester's jibe that the swine turned Norman when it became pork shows that the Saxon bears the toil while the Norman enjoys the fruit.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response denies the inequity Wamba describes, in which the living beast is Saxon and the served dish Norman.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies Wamba's argument that the brute goes by its Saxon name while in the charge of a Saxon slave, but becomes Norman when carried to the Castle-hall.

principles.source_thesis: Little is left to the Saxons but the air they breathe, reserved only to enable them to endure the tasks laid on their shoulders; the best and bravest supply their foreign masters with soldiers.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Saxons as prospering under Norman rule, contradicting Gurth's account of their condition.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies Gurth's argument that little is left to the Saxons but the air they breathe, and the best and bravest are sent to whiten distant lands with their bones.

principles.source_thesis: A fool who leads a guest to speak treason at disadvantage would be a knave to betray him; a fool cannot half so well help himself as a wise man.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the jester betray his companion's rash speech, contradicting the argument that betrayal would be the trick of a wise man, not a fool.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a jester will not betray one he has led into rash speech, since betrayal were the trick of a wise man.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer refuses reward for guiding the Jew, asking only that Isaac spare the gyves and dungeon to some unhappy Christian in his debt.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer demand money or advantage for his service, contradicting the argument that he desires no recompense.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the Palmer desires no recompense, asking only mercy for some unhappy Christian debtor.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer will protect a Jew against a Saracen, since to protect a Jew against a Saracen can scarce be accounted unworthy of a Christian.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer abandon the Jew to his pursuers as beneath his care, contradicting the argument that protecting him is not unworthy of a Christian.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a Christian may guide and in some sort defend a Jew against Saracen pursuers without dishonour.

principles.source_thesis: A knight errant may accept the loan of horse and armour from a Jew on the terms that they be returned after the tournament, or their value paid.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats accepting a loan of arms on honourable terms as beneath a knight, contradicting the text's account of the Palmer's bargain.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a knight may frankly use a Jew's courtesy in supplying horse and armour, and will requite it.

principles.source_thesis: The hermit's apparent abstinence is belied by his bluff countenance and by the hidden store of venison and wine, which he shares once ceremony is broken.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response presents the hermit as truly ascetic, contradicting the text's account of his concealed good cheer.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the hermit's fare of pease and water ill matches his brawny form, and that hidden provision appears once ceremony is broken.

principles.source_thesis: The hermit warns that it is dangerous to speak of spoiling the king's game, since he is true hermit to the king and law and would risk prison or hanging.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the hermit openly boast of poaching the king's deer, contradicting his warning against such dangerous words.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a hermit is true to the king and law and will not counsel spoiling the king's game.

principles.source_thesis: The Black Knight's offer to let the hermit name weapons, and the hermit's production of broadswords, bucklers, bows, and a harp, show that trial by equal arms may settle impertinent curiosity in friendship.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the hermit refuse all trial of arms or the knight decline it, contradicting the text's account of their proposed combat.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a host may offer equal arms in friendship and brotherly love to settle a guest's excess of curiosity.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's vow forbids him for a time to touch gold, and he will not accept the bracelet Cedric offers for naming the knights.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer accept gold in violation of his vow, contradicting the argument that his oath prohibits him from touching it.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a pilgrim under vow may refuse gold while freely telling what he witnessed.

principles.source_thesis: The Disinherited Knight refuses all ransom from the Templar and holds him in mortal defiance, while accepting ransom from the other knights and distributing it among squires, heralds, and minstrels.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the victor take ransom from the Templar or keep all ransom for himself, contradicting the text's account of his conduct.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the victor may refuse ransom from a mortal enemy while dealing generously with others and sharing the ransom with attendants.

principles.source_thesis: The Disinherited Knight will not profit by Rebecca's generosity, resolving that he will not take advantage of it.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the knight keep the Jewess's bounty for his own profit, contradicting the argument that he resolved not to profit by it.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a knight will not profit by a generosity that exceeds what was due, but will requite it.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's rebuke that those under oath to recover the holy city should not be found travelling far from the scene of their duties shames the Templar.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Templar's absence from the Holy Land as no reproach, contradicting the Palmer's rebuke.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that those sworn to recover the holy city may be reproached for travelling far from the scene of their duties.

principles.source_thesis: Cedric's vow binds him to advance no more than three steps from his dais to meet any who shares not Saxon royal blood, yet he receives Norman guests with dignified hospitality.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has Cedric abandon his vow of three steps or refuse the Normans entry, contradicting the text's account of his reception.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a host may keep his vow of limited ceremony while still receiving guests with dignified hospitality.

principles.source_thesis: Rowena's dignity in suppressing her sorrow, discovered only by her folded hands and tearless eye, moves even those not given to be moved by a woman's lament.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has Rowena give way to open lamentation, contradicting the text's account of her dignified suppression of sorrow.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that grief may be suppressed with such dignity that it is discovered only by folded hands and a tearless eye.

principles.source_thesis: The yeoman Locksley will not be compelled to shoot on an unfair wager, though the prince's power may strip and scourge him, but he obeys when the terms allow him a fair chance.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the yeoman submit to an unfair wager without protest, contradicting the argument that a man cannot be compelled to bend his bow on unfair terms.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a prince's power may strip and scourge a yeoman but cannot compel him to shoot on unfair terms, though he will obey fair ones.

principles.source_thesis: Locksley leaves the twenty nobles to Hubert, who drew as brave a bow as his grandsire, showing that a victor may forgo his prize in generosity to a modest competitor.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the victor keep all winnings and mock his rival, contradicting the text's account of Locksley's generosity to Hubert.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a victor may leave his prize to a modest competitor who did his best.

principles.source_thesis: Locksley vows that if ever he takes service, it shall be with King Richard, refusing Prince John's offer of livery and place.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the yeoman accept service with the usurping prince, contradicting the argument that his vow binds him to Richard alone.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a yeoman's vow of service to the true king cannot be bought by a prince's offer of livery.

principles.source_thesis: The Black Knight withdraws from the honours he has won, preferring to leave the field rather than receive the prize, and is termed the Black Sluggard for his indifference.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Black Knight remain to claim the prize and glory, contradicting the text's account of his self-denial.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a knight may achieve a great feat and then withdraw from the honours he has won, indifferent to reward.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's information that the Templar charged his slaves to seize the Jew shows that a warning given in time may save a man from a designed ambush.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer keep silent about the plot against Isaac, contradicting the argument that he came as a friend to warn him.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that one who learns of a designed ambush should warn the intended victim and guide him to safety.

principles.source_thesis: Isaac's dream of irons and torture reflects the real persecution of his people, whose persons and property were exposed to every turn of popular fury.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Jew's terror as groundless, contradicting the text's account of the relentless persecution of the Jews.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the Jew's terror is warranted, since his people were exposed to plunder and torture on the slightest pretences.

principles.source_thesis: Rebecca argues that the Gentiles, cruel as they are, depend on the dispersed children of Zion, and that the gold lent them returns with increase; the Jews are like the herb that flourishes most when trampled on.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Jews as wholly powerless and without advantage under persecution, contradicting Rebecca's argument.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies Rebecca's argument that the Jews have advantages even under persecution, since the Gentiles depend on their wealth and the gold returns with increase.

principles.source_thesis: Isaac's struggle between avarice and generosity, as he counts out the zecchins, shows a better nature contending with habitual love of gain.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response presents Isaac as purely avaricious without any struggle of generosity, contradicting the text's account of his divided feelings.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a miser's better nature may struggle with his avarice, urging him to restore part of what he has received.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's rebuke that it is discourteous to disturb a man's thoughts, and his guiding the party safely through bogs by instinct, show that a stranger may prove the truest guide.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Palmer's guidance as worthless or treacherous, contradicting the text's account of his safe conduct of the party.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a stranger who knows the passes may guide a party safely where others would be lost.

principles.source_thesis: Wamba's trick of misdirecting the Templar and Prior shows that a servant may use his wit to keep dangerous guests from his master's house without open quarrel.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the jester lead the dangerous guests straight to his master's house, contradicting the text's account of his misdirection.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a servant may use his wit to misdirect dangerous guests and prevent a quarrel with his master.

principles.source_thesis: The tournament laws provide that a knight breaking the rules of honourable chivalry shall be stript of his arms and his shield reversed in public derision.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats breaches of chivalric rules as without consequence, contradicting the proclaimed laws of the tournament.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a knight who transgresses the rules of honourable chivalry is liable to public derision and loss of arms.

principles.source_thesis: Prince John's design to name Rebecca Queen of Beauty is checked because no knight would lay lance in rest if such an insult were attempted, and his counsellors warn it would ruin his projects.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the prince's insulting design succeed without opposition, contradicting the text's account of the murmurs and warnings that checked him.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that wanton insult to the assembly would leave no knight willing to fight and would ruin the prince's projects.

principles.source_thesis: Athelstane's choice to fight on the Templar's side, from smothered displeasure at the victor's preference for Rowena, shows that private resentment may lead a man to injudicious party choice.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has Athelstane choose his party from pure principle, contradicting the text's account of his resentment-driven choice.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that private resentment may lead a man to an injudicious party choice which he cannot well justify.

principles.source_thesis: The Disinherited Knight's courtesy in declining to take advantage of De Grantmesnil's rearing horse wins him as much honour as his valour.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the knight press his advantage over the disordered horse, contradicting the text's account of his courtesy.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a champion may decline an accidental advantage and offer a second encounter, winning honour by courtesy as much as by address.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's rebuke to the Templar, that those under oath to recover the holy city should not be found far from their duties, is answered only by anger, since the reproach is just.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Templar's anger as a refutation of the Palmer's reproach, contradicting the argument that the reproach is just.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a just reproach to those who abandon their sworn duty may leave them only angry, not answered.

principles.source_thesis: The Black Knight thanks Saint Julian, the patron of travellers, for sending him good harbourage, showing that a traveller may piously acknowledge providential guidance.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the traveller's safe arrival as mere chance without acknowledgment, contradicting the text's account of his thanks to Saint Julian.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a traveller may thank the patron of travellers for sending him good harbourage.

principles.source_thesis: The hermit's claim that it has pleased Our Lady and his patron saint to bless his pittance, even as pulse and water were blessed to Shadrach, Meshech, and Abednego, defends his fare as miraculous.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response mocks the hermit's claim of miraculous blessing on his fare, contradicting his stated defense.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a hermit may hold his pittance blessed as the pulse and water were blessed to the children in the furnace.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal to speak in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall, though urged with good mead, shows that a vow of silence may be kept against courteous temptation.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer break his vow for a cup of mead, contradicting the text's account of his refusal.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a pilgrim's vow may oblige him to refuse to speak in the kitchen on matters prohibited in the hall.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's reply that he was born a native of these parts explains his perfect knowledge of the forest passes after long absence.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the guide's knowledge of the forest as impossible or suspicious without cause, contradicting the text's explanation.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a native of the parts may know the forest passes perfectly even after long absence.

principles.source_thesis: The Saxon franklin's vow and his pride in uninterrupted descent from Hereward make him a withstander of the nobility, so that courtesy must be used in approaching him.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats Cedric as servile toward the Norman nobility, contradicting the text's account of his pride and resistance.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a proud Saxon franklin stands up sternly for the privileges of his race and must be approached with courtesy.

principles.source_thesis: The Prior's wager with the Templar over Rowena's beauty, and the Templar's admission that he has seen no maiden so beautiful, show that even a vow-bound knight may be judged by his own word as a knight and churchman.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Templar deny the wager or judge falsely, contradicting the text's account of his honest admission.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a knight and churchman may be trusted to give true response on his word in a wager of beauty.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's rebuke that the Templar's threats are out of place in England, where islanders love not blows save those of holy Church, restrains the soldier's violence.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Prior allow the Templar to strike the peasant, contradicting the argument that islanders love not blows.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that violence against peasants is out of place in England, where blows are not loved save those of holy Church.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's warning that the Templar's Saracen slaves will regard neither territory nor manor nor lordship shows that a persecutor's reach may exceed the protection of law and boundary.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Jew as safe once beyond Front-de-Bœuf's boundary, contradicting the Palmer's warning.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that pursuers may regard neither territory nor manor nor lordship, so the Jew must not be left alone.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's insistence that he will see the Jew safe under fitting escort, since to protect a Jew against a Saracen can scarce be unworthy of a Christian, shows that charity may cross religious lines.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer abandon the Jew once out of immediate danger, contradicting the argument that he will see him safe under escort.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a Christian may guide and defend a Jew until he is safe under fitting escort.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal of recompense and his request that Isaac spare some unhappy Christian debtor show that mercy to debtors is a fit requital for kindness.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer demand repayment in money, contradicting the argument that he desires no recompense but mercy for a debtor.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the fit requital for kindness is to spare the gyves and dungeon to some unhappy debtor.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's smile at Isaac's guess that he lacks a horse and armour, and his admission that a knight's chain and spurs are hidden in his gown, show that a disguise may conceal a knight's true estate.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Palmer as truly a poor pilgrim without hidden estate, contradicting the text's account of his concealed knight's chain and spurs.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a pilgrim's gown may conceal a knight's chain and spurs, and that a sharp eye may guess what a man most lacks.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's caution that the steed may be slain and the armour injured, since he will spare neither horse nor man, shows that a borrower should honestly warn the lender of the risks.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer conceal the risks from Isaac, contradicting the argument that he warns him the steed may be slain and the armour injured.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a borrower should warn the lender that the horse may be slain and the armour injured, since he will spare neither.

principles.source_thesis: Isaac's better feelings prevail over his habitual caution when he supplies the knight despite the risk, showing that generosity may overcome avarice in a much-tried man.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has Isaac refuse the loan from avarice, contradicting the text's account of his better feelings prevailing.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a Jew's better feelings may prevail over his habitual caution, so that he supplies a knight despite the risk of loss.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's parting caution to the Jew not to thrust himself too forward into the vain hurly-burly, for the sake of his own life and limbs, shows that a friend may warn against vain risk.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer urge the Jew to seek danger, contradicting the argument that he warns him against vain risk.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a friend may caution another not to thrust himself too forward into a vain hurly-burly, for the sake of his life and limbs.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's guidance through devious paths, more than once exciting the Jew's suspicion that he intended betrayal, shows that a guide may be distrusted even while doing good.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Jew's suspicion as fully justified by the Palmer's conduct, contradicting the text's account of his faithful guidance.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a guide may be suspected of betrayal even while faithfully leading by the safest paths.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal to let the Jew pay him, and his acceptance of the loan of horse and armour on the terms of return or payment, show that a knight may deal honourably with a usurer.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the knight cheat the Jew of the loan, contradicting the argument that the arms are to be returned or their value paid.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a knight may accept a loan of arms on terms of return or payment and deal honourably with the lender.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's warning that the Templar's slaves will seize the Jew and conduct him to the castle of Malvoisin or Front-de-Bœuf shows that the great barons used their castles to extort from the Jews.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the barons' castles as places of justice rather than extortion, contradicting the text's account.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the great barons used their castles to extort hoards from the Jews by oppression and torture.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal to accept the Jew's thanks and his insistence that he desires no recompense show that a good deed may be done without thought of advantage.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer seek advantage from his good deed, contradicting the argument that he desires no recompense.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a good deed may be done without thought of advantage, and thanks alone may suffice.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's rebuke that Isaac blasphemes when he mocks Christian penance shows that a pilgrim may defend his faith while still aiding one of another faith.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer accept the Jew's mockery of his faith without rebuke, contradicting the text's account.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a pilgrim may sternly rebuke blasphemy while still guiding and defending the blasphemer.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's smile at Isaac's guess, and his warning that if Isaac's garments were searched by as curious an eye, discoveries might be made, show that each man may have secrets he would not have exposed.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Jew as having nothing to hide while the Palmer hides much, contradicting the text's account of mutual concealment.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that each man may have secrets, and a curious eye might make discoveries in the garments of either.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's insistence that he will not leave the Jew till he is under safe conduct of some chief or baron going to the tournament shows that protection may be sought through the goodwill of the powerful.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer abandon the Jew before safe conduct is secured, contradicting the argument that he will not leave him till then.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a guide will not leave a threatened man till he is under safe conduct of some powerful protector.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's assurance that the Jew may find many of his tribe at Sheffield with whom to take refuge shows that kin and community may provide safety where the powerful will not.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Jew as without any refuge among his own people, contradicting the text's account of his kinsman Zareth at Sheffield.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a persecuted man may find refuge among his own kin and tribe, as Isaac with his kinsman Zareth.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal of the Jew's offer to repay his good offices with money, and his request that Isaac spare some unhappy Christian debtor, show that mercy is a better requital than gold.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer accept gold as requital, contradicting the argument that mercy to a debtor is the fit requital.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that mercy to an unhappy debtor is a better requital than gold for a good office.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's warning that the Templar's slaves will watch the Jew's journey and seize him at a convenient distance shows that danger may be designed and timed by enemies.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats the Jew's danger as imaginary, contradicting the Palmer's specific warning of a designed seizure.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that enemies may watch a journey and seize a man at a convenient distance, so a timely warning is needed.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's guidance by secret paths known as well to him as to any forester shows that knowledge of the country may be a form of protection.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats knowledge of secret paths as useless for protection, contradicting the text's account of the Palmer's guidance.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that knowledge of secret forest paths may protect a fugitive from pursuers.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal to let the Jew travel in Cedric's train, because Saxon or Norman will be equally ashamed of the poor Israelite, shows that protection may be denied by those who would not injure.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response treats Cedric as willing to protect the Jew in his train, contradicting the text's account of the shame that would prevent it.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that Saxon and Norman alike would be ashamed to travel with a Jew, so protection must be sought elsewhere.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's warning that the Jew's dream of irons and torture is not dreamed for nought, since his brethren have been used to extort their hoards, shows that persecution is real and foreseen.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response dismisses the Jew's fear as superstition, contradicting the Palmer's confirmation that he has cause for terror.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that the Jew has cause for terror, considering how his brethren have been used to extort their hoards by princes and nobles.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's compassion for the Jew is mingled with contempt, showing that aid may be given without esteem.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response presents the Palmer's aid as flowing from esteem, contradicting the text's account of compassion mingled with contempt.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that one may aid a distressed man while viewing his distress with compassion in which contempt is largely mingled.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal to accept contamination from the Jew's touch, while still aiding him, shows that aid may be given at a distance without close fellowship.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer embrace the Jew in close fellowship, contradicting the text's account of his shrinking from the touch.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that one may aid a man while declining close fellowship, extricating himself as if there were contamination in the touch.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's assurance that he is vowed to poverty and will not change his dress save for a horse and coat of mail shows that a vow may be kept while still preparing for combat.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer abandon his vow of poverty for gain, contradicting the text's account of his vow.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a pilgrim vowed to poverty may yet change his dress for a horse and coat of mail when combat requires it.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's warning that the Jew's journey may prove dangerous, and his offer to guide him by secret paths, show that a timely warning and guidance may save a man from designed harm.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer warn the Jew but then refuse to guide him, contradicting the text's account of his offer.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that one who warns of danger should also offer guidance to safety.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's refusal to accept the Jew's money, and his request that Isaac spare some unhappy Christian debtor, show that a good office may be requited by mercy rather than by payment.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer demand payment for his guidance, contradicting the argument that mercy is the fit requital.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a good office may be requited by sparing an unhappy debtor rather than by payment.

principles.source_thesis: The Palmer's guidance of the Jew through the forest, and his parting at Sheffield, show that a helper may leave a man at the threshold of safety among his own people.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response has the Palmer abandon the Jew in the wilderness, contradicting the text's account of his guidance to Sheffield.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the argument that a guide may conduct a threatened man to the threshold of safety among his own people and then part from him.

principles.source_thesis: Hospitality and generosity toward the despised and the enemy are owed as a Christian duty; Rowena insists that 'Jews though they be, we cannot as Christians leave them in this extremity,' and Rebecca appeals that in wounds and misery 'the Gentile becometh the Jew's brother.'
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold the claim that Christians owe mercy and protection even to despised Jews in extremity, or where it endorses Athelstane's refusal of aid.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the text's argument that mercy must be shown to the outcast and the enemy, citing Rowena's and Rebecca's appeals as the standard.

principles.source_thesis: A true knight's duty is to defend the weaker party and the oppressed; the Black Knight says 'Such is the duty of a true knight at least' and calls chivalry 'the stay of the oppressed, the redresser of grievances, the curb of the power of the tyrant.'
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response contradicts the text's claim that knighthood obliges the strong to rescue the weak and curb tyrants, rather than serve ambition.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the text's view that a true knight is bound to aid the weaker party and redress oppression, as the Black Knight and Ivanhoe argue.

principles.source_thesis: Fidelity and self-sacrifice for one's master are honorable even in a fool; Wamba offers to die in Cedric's stead, and Cedric declares his memory 'shall be preserved while fidelity and affection have honour upon earth.'
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response dismisses Wamba's sacrifice or treats loyal service as mere folly unworthy of honor.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it honors Wamba's willing self-sacrifice and Cedric's vow to preserve his memory, as the text presents fidelity as honorable.

principles.source_thesis: Freedom is a good that transforms a man; Gurth, freed and given land, cries 'A smith and a file to do away the collar from the neck of a freeman!' and feels 'a free spirit in my breast.'
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats servitude as natural or freedom as worthless, contradicting the text's celebration of Gurth's manumission.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it affirms the text's claim that liberty ennobles and strengthens a faithful man, as shown in Gurth's emancipation.

principles.source_thesis: Even outlaws may keep just laws and civil discipline among themselves; Locksley divides spoil impartially, sets aside a tenth for the church and portions for widows, and the Black Knight marvels that 'men, in a state so lawless, were nevertheless among themselves so regularly and equitably governed.'
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response denies that lawless men can act justly or equitably, contradicting the text's portrait of Locksley's ordered band.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reflect the text's argument that justice and discipline can exist even among outlaws, as in Locksley's impartial division of spoil.

principles.source_thesis: He who has power to do evil and does good deserves praise; the Black Knight says 'he that does good, having the unlimited power to do evil, deserves praise not only for the good which he performs, but for the evil which he forbears.'
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response fails to recognize the merit of forbearing evil when one has power to commit it, contrary to the Black Knight's maxim.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it embodies the principle that restraint from evil, where one has power to do it, is itself praiseworthy, as the Black Knight tells Locksley.

principles.source_thesis: Paternal affection is natural even in a despised people; Isaac cries that 'the hunted fox, the tortured wildcat loves its young—the despised and persecuted race of Abraham love their children!' and refuses ransom unless his daughter is freed in honor.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response denies that Jews possess natural parental love or treats Isaac's love for Rebecca as mere avarice.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it affirms, as the text does, that Isaac's love for his daughter is natural and powerful, surpassing even his love of wealth.

principles.source_thesis: Honor must be preferred to life; Rebecca stands on the parapet declaring she will rather trust her soul to God than her honor to the Templar, and Ivanhoe holds that chivalry 'teaches us to fear no evil but disgrace.'
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response counsels submission to dishonor for safety's sake, contradicting Rebecca's and Ivanhoe's resolve to prefer death to disgrace.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it upholds the text's claim that honor is to be preferred above life, as Rebecca and Ivanhoe both insist.

principles.source_thesis: Vengeance and remorse without repentance destroy the soul; Ulrica's guilt and Front-de-Bœuf's deathbed show that 'remorse without repentance' is a fearful state, and Cedric bids her repent rather than despair.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats revenge as sweet or guilt as harmless, contradicting the text's warning in Ulrica's and Front-de-Bœuf's fates.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it reflects the text's warning that vengeance and unrepented guilt bring despair, and that repentance, not revenge, is the remedy.

principles.source_thesis: A vow or pledged word must be kept even by the flawed; Bois-Guilbert swears 'my word never' was broken, and De Bracy holds himself 'true prisoner, rescue or no rescue.'
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats pledged faith as dispensable, contradicting the text's insistence that even wicked men hold their word inviolate.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it honors the text's principle that a pledged word binds, as Bois-Guilbert and De Bracy both maintain.

principles.source_thesis: Pride and habitual domination are a false character that deserts one in real danger; Rowena's haughtiness is 'a fictitious character' that quails when opposed by a determined mind, and she is saved by humility and appeal to Heaven.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response praises haughty self-will as true courage, contrary to the text's exposure of Rowena's pride as a mask that fails her.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it reflects the text's view that true fortitude lies in humility and reliance on Heaven, not in proud self-assertion.

principles.source_thesis: The oppressed Saxons' cause of national restoration is noble, yet Cedric's willingness to sacrifice his son's happiness to it is shown as a painful cost; the text presents his patriotism as sincere but costly.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response either condemns Saxon patriotism outright or ignores the human cost Cedric's cause exacts, contrary to the text's balanced portrayal.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so it presents Saxon restoration as a noble but costly cause, as the text does through Cedric's sacrifice of domestic happiness.

principles.source_thesis: Religious vows and the rules of an order bind the sworn member absolutely; a vowed soldier of the Temple must sacrifice ease, comforts, and natural affections, and many pleasures lawful to others are forbidden to him.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats a sworn knight's private desires or worldly pleasures as legitimate grounds for action, thereby contradicting the text's claim that the vowed Templar is bound beyond what is lawful to other men.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it affirms that the sworn soldier of the Temple must renounce ease, comforts, and natural affections, and that pleasures lawful to others are forbidden to him by his calling.

principles.source_thesis: The Order's decline is caused by wealth, luxury, presumption, and license, and its survival requires casting away riches and reforming manners sharply and suddenly, not cautiously.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response excuses or minimizes the corruption of the Order through wealth and indulgence, or recommends only cautious gradual reform, contrary to Beaumanoir's argument that the reformation must be sharp and sudden.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it names luxury, wealth, and license as the causes of the Order's peril and insists that these must be cast away and manners reformed sharply and suddenly to avert its destruction.

principles.source_thesis: A leader's authority is symbolized by the staff and the rod: the staff to support the weak, the rod to correct delinquents; brethren may not walk by their own will but by the Master's.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats a subordinate brother's private judgment or independent action as rightful against his Superior, contradicting the text's claim that the staff and rod belong to the Master and that a Preceptor may not walk according to his own will.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it upholds the Master's authority to support the weak with the staff and correct delinquents with the rod, and denies that a brother may act according to his own will rather than his Superior's.

principles.source_thesis: Suspected sorcery is to be treated as the devil's deception, and the accused instrument of Satan's power over a knight is to bear the full weight of punishment, even where the knight is pitied as a victim.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats healing arts or the accused woman as innocent and harmless, ignoring the text's argument that such practices are demonic deceptions and that the accursed instrument must be punished.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it treats the alleged charms and cures as the deceptions of the devouring Enemy and holds that the instrument of a knight's fall must be punished while the erring knight is rather pitied than chastised.

principles.source_thesis: A defenceless stranger who claims the benefit of the Order's mild laws, including trial by combat, must not be refused it, since knights and men of religion would be shamed to refuse proffered combat.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response would deny an accused stranger the trial by combat or treat her claim to it as void because of her faith, contradicting the Grand Master's stated refusal to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of the laws.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it grants the accused stranger the trial by combat she demands, on the grounds that it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat or to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of their mild laws.

principles.source_thesis: Innocence cast into the scale outweighs force: the silk glove of an innocent accuser outweighs the iron gauntlet of the Order, and God will show the right in combat.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the accused's weakness or her people's low standing as proof against her, rather than weighing her innocence against the power arrayed against her.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it weighs the accused's innocence in the scale and affirms that the frail gage of an innocent woman may outweigh the iron gauntlet of a powerful order, leaving the judgment to God.

principles.source_thesis: No spell can affect the champion who comes forward to fight for the judgment of God; the combat's issue is God's judgment, not human strength.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response attributes the outcome of the combat to mere human skill, fatigue, or chance rather than to the judgment of God, contradicting the text's claim that no spell can affect the champion who fights for God's judgment.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it presents the combat as an appeal to God's judgment, in which no enchantment can affect the champion and the outcome is God's will rather than human prowess.

principles.source_thesis: A woman of courage may show more fortitude in suffering than a warrior in battle; the courage of a woman called to suffer by affection or duty may mount higher than the fighter's.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the accused woman as too weak or fearful to endure, ignoring Rebecca's argument that a woman's courage in suffering may exceed a warrior's in battle.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it acknowledges that a tenderly nurtured woman, fearful of danger and impatient of pain, may yet show courage in suffering that mounts higher than the warrior's in his fiercest battles.

principles.source_thesis: Deliverance must not be sold: protection of the oppressed must be given for charity's sake, not for a selfish requital, and a deed of generosity must not be bartered for a price.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response makes the rescue of the oppressed conditional on a reward or personal requital, contradicting the text's insistence that protection be given for charity and not for selfish advantage.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it insists the oppressed be protected for the sake of charity alone, refusing any bargain in which deliverance is sold for a price or personal requital.

principles.source_thesis: Faith is not to be changed like a garment unsuited to the climate; one may die for the law of one's fathers rather than abandon it.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response urges abandoning one's inherited faith for safety or advantage, contradicting Rebecca's claim that she may not change the faith of her fathers like a garment and can die for it if it be God's will.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it upholds steadfastness in the faith of one's fathers, refusing to treat conversion as a garment to be changed for safety, and accepting that one may die for it if such is God's will.

principles.source_thesis: Men throw on fate the issue of their own wild passions; wrongdoing is not excused by calling it destiny.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response excuses a person's harmful choices by appealing to fate or irresistible fatality, contradicting Rebecca's charge that men throw on fate the issue of their own wild passions.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it refuses to excuse wrongdoing as fate, affirming instead that men attribute to destiny the consequences of their own untamed passions.

principles.source_thesis: The persecution of the Jews has driven them to usury and money-dealing, but their ancient lineage and former glory are not erased by that degradation.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the Jewish people as naturally miserly or base, ignoring Rebecca's argument that persecution drove them to usury and that their descent from the princes of the House of Jacob remains.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it acknowledges that oppression has left the Jews only the road of industry and money-dealing, while affirming that their ancient names and lineage are not shamed by that condition.

principles.source_thesis: Forgiveness may be freely granted even to one who has caused deadly harm; the victim may forgive as freely as ever victim forgave her executioner.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response withholds forgiveness or demands vengeance from the wronged person, contradicting Rebecca's free forgiveness of Bois-Guilbert despite his being the author of her early death.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that the wronged person freely forgives the one who harmed her, granting pardon without requiring vengeance or satisfaction.

principles.source_thesis: A king's clemency and personal generosity are praised, yet a ruler's careless and wilfully indulgent administration is a defect; the lion preys not on prostrate carcasses, but royal mercy may invite treason.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats a ruler's clemency as simply a virtue without noting the text's observation that such indulgence may invite treason and that careless administration is a defect.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it praises the king's refusal to prey on a prostrate enemy while also acknowledging that careless and over-indulgent rule may invite treason and neglect the welfare of the kingdom.

principles.source_thesis: A prince who exposes his own person to rash adventures while his kingdom is threatened with civil war neglects his subjects, who are menaced when deprived of their sovereign.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response praises a ruler's personal adventures without weighing the text's charge that such rash exposure endangers the kingdom and leaves subjects menaced by civil war.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it recognizes that a sovereign's rash adventures, however brave, endanger his kingdom and subjects, and that his first care should be the welfare of those who depend on him.

principles.source_thesis: Reconciliation between former enemies and the union of two peoples is a public good, to be preferred to the pride of ancient quarrels and the hope of civil war.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response prefers the pride of an ancient quarrel or the prospect of civil war to reconciliation and union, contradicting the text's praise of the marriage as a pledge of future peace and harmony between the races.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it values reconciliation and union between former enemies as a public good, setting aside the pride of ancient quarrels and the hope of civil war.

principles.source_thesis: A man of his word must keep faith even when the promise was made to one of an opposing race; Cedric keeps his pledge to a Norman.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats a promise made to an opponent or outsider as not binding, contradicting the text's insistence that the son of Hereward knows how to keep his word even when passed to a Norman.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it affirms that a pledge must be kept even when given to one of an opposing people, and that breaking it would make a man faithless and man-sworn.

principles.source_thesis: Ambition is the serious business of life while women are but toys of lighter hours; yet the text shows such cold counsel leading to a man's death by his own contending passions.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response endorses Malvoisin's counsel to cast off the woman for the sake of ambition without noting that the text presents Bois-Guilbert's death as the fruit of his contending passions.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it does not simply endorse the cold counsel of ambition over affection, but shows that a man who abandons another to her fate for rank and ambition may be destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions.

principles.source_thesis: Hypocrisy that wears the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it is a vice distinct from open audacity, and the text marks such men as unprincipled.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats a hypocrite who feigns ascetic devotion while privately despising it as admirable or harmless, contrary to the text's characterization of such dissolute and unprincipled men.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it exposes the hypocrisy of one who assumes the exterior of fanaticism while inwardly despising it, and refuses to credit such a man with genuine devotion.

principles.source_thesis: A judge who has determined the sentence beforehand makes trial move rapidly; justice that is a foregone conclusion is not justice.
